EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small sedan attempted to ford Tres Pinos Creek along Browns Valley Road near Paicines on the night of February 17, with first responders responding to the scene during the night. The next morning, the driver was found walking along Highway 25 asking about the location of the passenger. The passenger's body was eventually found a mile downstream of where the car had gotten stranded. The driver was later arrested on charges of gross vehicular manslaughter. At the time of the incident, the TESC1 river gauge on Tres Pinos Creek measured stages above 2 feet, compared to a typical stage of less than a foot.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cyclone approached the Central Coast on February 10, resulting in the first substantial rainfall in over a month for much of the Bay Area and Central Coast. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.

The river then receded back below bankfull level late that night. Impacts included flooding of County Route 39 near the bridge heading out of town.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding observed on Stillwell Road and Pristine Pointe.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, however precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon.||In the first twenty-four hours of the event, precipitation amounts ranged from around half an inch to two inches across northern West Virginia. Meanwhile, amounts generally remained under an inch within the southern half of the state. Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. Rises on local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers primarily led to flooded roads in Wood, Gilmer, and Ritchie Counties on the 4th, then runoff prompted minor flooding to develop on the Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek the morning of the 6th. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off during the day.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The most significant impact occurred south of Orofino, where a large landslide blocked US-12 between mile markers 44 and 45. The initial slide occurred around 1539MST on Friday, March 13. While crews worked to clear the route, a second slide occurred at the same location at 0920MST on Saturday, March 14. The highway remained closed in both directions until Saturday afternoon. Additional landslides and rockslides were reported on Lower Fords Creek Road, Grangemont Road, Sunnyside, and Bobbitt Bench. Heavy traffic diverted to Sunnyside Road caused that secondary route to begin failing under the saturated conditions.||In Orofino, the urban drainage system reached maximum capacity and overflowed, flooding residential areas. In the Riverside area (115th Street), rushing water surrounded homes and filled basements. Significant damage occurred at the Joint School District 171 bus garage when a nearby creek (likely Flume Creek) blew out, flooding the facility. While officials successfully moved most of the fleet, one school bus and a neighboring food pantry were inundated and suffered major damage.||Small streams and creeks, including Jim Fords Creek and Freeman Creek, crested their banks, threatening homes and washing out culverts. Near Weippe, a creek overflowed onto the roadway, causing significant rutting. The Clearwater River at Orofino saw a dramatic rise of over 8 feet, increasing from 5.78 feet on Thursday to a crest of 13.96 feet on Saturday night   staying just below the 16-foot flood stage, though the high water contributed to the drainage backup in the city. Total rainfall between March 10 and 15 included 3.57 in Orofino, 4.00 in Peck, and 4.50 at the Pierce SNOTEL.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense and prolonged atmospheric river (AR) impacted the Northern Rockies, directed primarily at North-Central Idaho. This event was characterized by a deep moisture plume and an unseasonably warm air mass, which transitioned mountain snow to a heavy rain-on-snow event. Total precipitation across the Clearwater Basin ranged from 2.5 to over 5.0 inches.  Impacts from this storm included power outages and impacts to travel.  The biggest impact, however, was flooding in Clearwater County near Orofino.  By the morning of March 13, several days of moderate rain and mild temperatures had completely saturated the soil. With the ground unable to absorb any more water and temperatures remaining above freezing overnight, continued rainfall and rapid snowmelt triggered immediate runoff. This surge of water overwhelmed culverts, destabilized hillsides, and caused rapid rises on small streams and the Clearwater River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread low-land flooding occurred in Outagamie County, resulting in considerable flood damage along the Wolf River and Embarrass River to 52 homes and $4.6 million of damage. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days.  Power and gas in these areas were shutoff as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of heavy precipitation events resulted in record setting and historic flooding on several rivers across northeast Wisconsin from the middle to late part of April. The heavy rainfall especially impacted the Wolf River basin, leading to record setting flooding for the Wolf River at Shiocton and the Wolf River at New London. Record flooding also occurred on other rivers over northeast Wisconsin, including the Embarrass River. ||The river flooding resulted in tremendous disruptions to daily life for those living along and near the Wolf River and Embarrass River. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days. Power and gas were shutoff in these areas as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses. The peak of the flooding along the Wolf River occurred from April 16 through April 21.  Flooding then moved downstream on the Wolf River, impacting the Fremont area. Over 150 homes were affected, with damages estimated over $4 million.

The environment south of the front featured robust moisture, strong instability, and sufficient wind shear. Wind shear was further maximized in the vicinity of the warm front, resulting in a localized corridor of higher tornado potential. Supercell thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and continued into the evening. These storms produced all severe hazards, but the most common hazard was large hail, the largest of which was two inches in diameter in Mason County. A brief tornado occurred in Tazewell County. Training thunderstorms resulted in a narrow corridor of heavy rain from Fulton to Tazewell County, where several reports of flooded roadways were received. Radar estimates suggested 2 to 4 inches of rain fell in these areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 25th ahead of a slow-moving cold front situated near the Ohio River, with precipitable water values reaching into the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the Southside area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis. Abundant daytime heating allowed CAPE values to reach in excess of 1,500 J/kg during the evening. A line of slow-moving thunderstorms developed along a nearly-stationary surface trough that extended from Carroll County through central Halifax and Charlotte Counties, with multiple cells observed training along this boundary. The heaviest rain was observed within the Polecat Creek and Miry Creek basins, where nearly 5.5 inches fell within a 3-hour period. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to be producing rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour. Cells began to develop over the basins at around 6:00 pm EDT, with training reaching a maximum at around 8:00 pm EDT. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D3: Extreme Drought highlighted for all of Halifax County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 200-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration along a east-west strip within the west-central portion of the county, with rainfall totals reaching 150 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 350 to 650 cfs per mi^2 during the storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Southeast Michigan during the late afternoon and early evening of April 4. This triggered two lines of thunderstorms that caused pockets of damage south of I-94. The most significant storm occurred in Wayne County, producing an EF-1 tornado in Van Buren Township. The system also dumped 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some areas seeing up to 4 inches. Because the region had already received 3 to 5 inches over the previous five days, these additional downpours caused the Tittabawassee, Clinton, and Flint rivers to overflow. In addition, significant localized flooding occurred on already saturated ground, with the hardest-hit area being northwest Oakland County, specifically in and around Holly.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm storm brought mountain snow-melt, heavy rain and gusty winds as a potent low pressure system pushed across the area March 16-17th.  This caused some minor ice jams, but no ice left its banks during this event.  Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches fell over the 36 hour period leading to rapid stream and river rises across the state.  A few rivers reached minor flood stage, with most other rivers remaining just below flood stage or in action stage.  Long term drought helped mitigate flood conditions as base flow river levels where very low.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave advancing through the Ohio Valley and Pennsylvania allowed for a complex of thunderstorms to develop across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours of June 10, 2026. Upscale growth of this complex continued into portions of central Pennsylvania where slightly more moisture and instability was in place, with CAPE values peaking between 2000-3000 J/kg during the afternoon hours across much of the region. Storms largely stayed below severe limits due to the lack of bulk shear; however, some strong-to-severe thunderstorms knocked down trees in northern York County. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall occurred during portions of Mifflin County, where ponding of water occurred due to a slow-moving thunderstorm ahead of this complex with additional rainfall occurring during the afternoon hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a wet month for much of Central NY (CNY), especially around the Finger Lakes region, as precipitation was 150%-200% of normal. Several reports of river flooding occurred during the first couple of days of the month due to heavy rainfall. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moisture associated with Tropical Storm Arthur approached Central Alabama on June 17 into June 18. On June 17, several showers and low-topped supercells developed over southeastern Central Alabama. One cell produced a well-defined funnel cloud in southeastern Lowndes County that was caught in at least two videos posted to social media. The next day, heavy rainfall near Chalkville led to a portion of Sweeny Hollow Rd being flooded.||In the wake of the remnants of Arthur passing through Central Alabama on June 18, a cold front entered the area and became stalled. On June 19, heavy rainfall became concentrated along a boundary along and south of the U.S. 80 corridor, leading to flooding issues in Pike and Lowndes counties. By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant amounts of snowmelt on still-frozen ground, coupled with multiple rounds of heavy rainfall resulting in 4-7 inches of rainfall across the entirety of the county, resulted in significant and widespread flooding in Cheboygan County. Emergency management put out a statement by mid-month that all roads in Cheboygan county had some portion covered in water, with not enough road closed signs to go around; the sheriff's office stated nearly every waterway in the county have overflowed beyond their banks, swallowing docks, roads, yards, and in far too many cases, homes. Homes and businesses along the Sturgeon River near Wolverine were damaged by flooding, and around 200 homes in Indian River were damaged by flooding, with one homeowner reporting his refrigerator was definitely floating at one point. The three largest inland lakes across the Tip of the Mitt region -- Burt, Mullett, and Black Lakes -- all had high water levels with damage resulting to surrounding homes and roads due to flooding. The high water levels, coupled with strong winds, allowed for an ice shove, where lingering lake ice piled up into many homes on the downwind side of the lake, causing further damage beyond flooding alone. The Cheboygan Dam, a significant-risk dam 1.5 miles from the outlet of the Cheboygan River (the outlet for all lakes/rivers in Cheboygan county) and 0.75 miles from downtown Cheboygan and US-23, was under intense scrutiny for concerns of being overtopped due to the significant amounts of water in the basin, and the US-23 bascule bridge in Cheboygan was raised on April 13 due to debris concerns; this stayed up for several days, resulting in detoured traffic and economic impacts to businesses in the community. Dams further upstream in the basin, including the Alverno and Kleber Dams on the Black River, were also scrutinized and repaired as needed to keep water from surging downstream into the Cheboygan Dam, and a hydroelectric power generation plant at the Cheboygan Dam complex was quickly repaired and restarted to further aid in increasing flows through the dam. The dam's highest peak was just over 6 inches from the top. A levee on the Little Black River north of Cheboygan was breached on the 14th, unrelated to the Cheboygan Dam concerns, and resulted in evacuations on the north edge of the city of Cheboygan. Flooding continued into mid-May.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm temperatures during early April began to melt 2-3 feet of dense snowpack that had fallen across parts of northern Michigan in the historic mid-March winter storm, including Beaver Island. Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across northern Michigan through mid-April as well, resulting in total rainfall through the month of April across northern Michigan ranging from 5 to as much as nearly 16 inches at the Wellston Tippy Dam cooperative observing site in southeastern Manistee county. Traverse City, Houghton Lake, and Gaylord all recorded their wettest Aprils on record. Coupled with thawing ground and saturated soils, this resulted in widespread historic flooding across all of the northern Lower Peninsula. 20 USGS river gauges in the region set new all-time records, most of which broke the previous records by 1-2 feet. This, too, resulted in enhanced concern for multiple high-impact dams to be overtopped, including the Cheboygan Dam in the town of Cheboygan, which reached a height of just under 6 inches from the top at its peak, and the Bellaire Dam in northwest Lower Michigan. Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level trough moved into the Rockies on May 18, with southwest flow aloft over the Missouri Ozarks. A cluster of thunderstorms pushed southeast into portions of central Missouri, bringing heavy rainfall and flash flooding to St. Clair, Benton, and Camden counties. Additionally, a low level jet axis extending from the Gulf through eastern Kansas strengthened overnight into May 19 while interacting with the upper level trough and a surface front. As a result, a second line of thunderstorms formed across northern Kansas, moving into Missouri overnight before exiting the state in the late afternoon hours. With the multiple rounds of heavy rainfall, storm total rainfall observations ranged between 3-7 inches across portions of southeast Kansas and the Missouri Ozarks, with 8.20 inches of rainfall measured in Hickory County. This led to multiple road closures reported from the flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex of thunderstorms that pushed through the region during the morning of April 27th led to a period of stable conditions before additional thunderstorms began developing ahead of an approaching cold front by late afternoon.  With the atmosphere becoming considerably more unstable and sheared, some of the initial cells produced hail as large as ping pong balls (1.5 in diameter) between the Illinois River and I-55.  The storms quickly consolidated into a line, then swept eastward into Indiana by mid-evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred along the line, with a swath of higher winds and enhanced damage along a path from Mount Pulaski in southern Logan County northeastward to near Mahomet in northern Champaign County.  A National Weather Service Lincoln storm survey revealed 5 EF-1 tornado touchdowns within this area, resulting in sporadic tree, power line, and minor structural damage.  In addition to the severe convection, copious rainfall occurred on April 27th...with widespread amounts of 2-4 inches along and south of the I-72 corridor.  The heaviest rain occurred from southern Shelby County southeastward to Crawford County where 4 to 6 inches were common.  Due to excessive rainfall rates, scattered flash flooding was observed...with the most significant flooding near Herrick and Cowden in southern Shelby County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread high water affected the Flathead River basin. Anticipating heavy rainfall, operators at the Hungry Horse Dam opened the spillway gates at 1137MST on May 28 to manage reservoir capacity, causing significant downstream rises. On Friday morning, May 28, the City of Columbia Falls temporarily closed the back portion of River's Edge Park to the public due to early inundation. The Flathead River at Columbia Falls (CFMM8) crested at 13.78 feet with a discharge of 46,400 CFS on the evening of May 29, remaining above the minor flood stage of 13.0 feet. A subsequent NWS flood survey on June 1 at 1025MST documented high water completely surrounding private residential properties near the confluence of the South Fork and Middle Fork of the Flathead River. Floodwaters fully encircled a home 1 mile west of Hungry Horse, though the water had not yet breached the structural foundation or entered the living spaces at the time of the inspection.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between May 28 and June 4, 2026, a very slow-moving upper-level low-pressure system  over Montana tapped into moisture from the Gulf of America, bringing heavy and widespread precipitation to western Montana. Prior to this event, several locations had already received significant moisture in May, leaving soils saturated and mountain runoff elevated. The combination of intense rainfall and ongoing snowmelt led to swollen rivers, and overwhelmed small streams, and flooded local irrigation canals. Intense thunderstorms brought heavy rain-rates in Sanders County resulting in mudslides.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread small stream, agricultural, and infrastructural flooding occurred across the Mission Valley due to accelerated snowmelt and 4 to 6 inches of rainfall over a four-day period. A private weather station located 3 miles east-northeast of Pablo measured a total of 5.09 inches of rain from Friday through Monday, while another station just north of the Mission Reservoir measured 3.46 inches. Initial minor flooding began on Friday evening, May 29, when a storm dropped 0.50 to 0.60 inches of rain along the eastern side of the valley, flooding one-third of a private property near St. Ignatius. Runoff rapidly filled local irrigation systems, causing widespread issues.  |At 0600MST on May 31, the lower cylinder flood gate at Mission Dam failed during a high-flow period. While flows were already elevated, this mechanical failure induced a dynamic flow condition where discharges dropped momentarily until emergency teams opened the upper cylinder gate to stabilize the dam, returning outflow into Mission Creek to approximately 350 CFS. At 1000MST, Agency Creek breached its banks, flooding low-lying pastures between Jocko and Agency Roads. At 1300MST, North Crow Creek overflowed, inundating properties along Minesinger Trail. |At 1430MST, the Pablo Feeder Canal experienced a structural failure at Skyline Drive and Caffrey Road, flooding adjacent crop fields. A multi-agency emergency response deployed heavy equipment and placed over 500 sandbags to reinforce the canal's south wall and repair the road base. |On June 1, NWS storm surveys documented extensive field flooding along Red Horn, Hillside, and Foothills Roads due to out-of-bank tributaries. North Crow Creek completely left its banks around Timberlane Road, inundating driveways and spreading water within 1 to 2 feet of a home's foundation. Floodwaters along the Pablo Feeder Canal completely submerged a length of Minesinger Trail and Mountain View Road, rendering them impassable to traffic. At 1400MST on June 1, with the Kicking Horse Reservoir at full capacity, all active water diversions from South Crow into the reservoir ceased. This forced the unbuffered, full natural flow from the South Crow drainage directly downstream into Crow Creek. The resulting surge caused Crow Creek to leave its banks entirely, backing up directly into a commercial greenhouse business (Bev's Bloomers). The floodwaters came within one foot of an adjacent home's foundation, and left a 6-foot property fence completely underwater. Severe road washouts were also reported north of Arlee on Saddle Mountain Road, where heavy rains stripped away soil and gravel to expose bedrock. Debris, mud, and water gushed across Highway MT-35 at milepost 10 on Monday evening, carrying a boulder the size of a small car onto the driving lanes near Woods Bay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped south into the region and combined with a warm, moist and unstable airmass to bring isolated showers and thunderstorms to the region on the afternoon and evening of June 13. Storms primarily affected the east and northeast Texas Panhandle with damaging winds and small hail.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Warm weather following the historic 2-3ft wet, dense snowfall from the Mid-March Winter Storm led to snowmelt, and over the course of the month, an additional 5-7 inches of rainfall fell across the county, resulting in significant and widespread flooding; a state of emergency for Emmet county was declared by the 15th, and flooding impacts across the county continued into the month of May. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. Two portions of M-119, the Tunnel of Trees along the coastline of Lake Michigan between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, were closed due to washouts:  the stretch from Terpening Rd to West Stutsmanville Rd was closed due to a significant washout on the steep slopes near the road, leaving the roadway compromised and closed through at least summer. South of Cross Village, a culvert was overwhelmed, causing the roadway to fail completely, and will also remain closed for much of the summer. Significant flooding impacts were noted in Pellston, Petoskey, Alanson, Cross Village, and the Crooked River Locks.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm temperatures during early April began to melt 2-3 feet of dense snowpack that had fallen across parts of northern Michigan in the historic mid-March winter storm, including Beaver Island. Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across northern Michigan through mid-April as well, resulting in total rainfall through the month of April across northern Michigan ranging from 5 to as much as nearly 16 inches at the Wellston Tippy Dam cooperative observing site in southeastern Manistee county. Traverse City, Houghton Lake, and Gaylord all recorded their wettest Aprils on record. Coupled with thawing ground and saturated soils, this resulted in widespread historic flooding across all of the northern Lower Peninsula. 20 USGS river gauges in the region set new all-time records, most of which broke the previous records by 1-2 feet. This, too, resulted in enhanced concern for multiple high-impact dams to be overtopped, including the Cheboygan Dam in the town of Cheboygan, which reached a height of just under 6 inches from the top at its peak, and the Bellaire Dam in northwest Lower Michigan. Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant, widespread flooding occurred across Antrim county due to snowmelt and 6-12 inches of rainfall through the course of the month, most of which fell in a few days in the middle of the month. This resulted in damage to businesses, homes, and roadways, with significant home foundation damage estimates as high as $50,000 to $100,000 per house. Some erosion under a berm along the Bellaire Dam was noticed on the 13th, resulting in emergency repairs and monitoring as water levels behind the dam reached the highest peak in its recorded 100 year history:  lake levels on Intermediate Lake, upstream from the Bellaire Dam, rose from 8.61ft on the 11th to 10.38ft on the morning of the 14th, and a discharge rate of 90,000 gallons per minute through the dam was not enough to lower river levels during the peak of the flooding. Water came within 12 inches of overtopping the dam...with additional concerns over a culvert upstream near Ellsworth. Residents of much of the town of Bellaire were put on alert from the 13th through the 19th for potential evacuations as a result.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant, widespread flooding due to snowmelt and a monthly total of 7-15 inches of rain across the county, resulted in an emergency declaration for the county. The culverts for the Boardman River beneath Beitner Rd, a major road carrying 20-40,000 vehicles per day south of Traverse City, were overwhelmed on the evening of the 14th, resulting in total bridge failure in a matter of a few minutes; the USGS river gauge at this site was also swept away. Downstream, at the former Union St. Dam/new FishPass site, the river came within a half inch of meeting the 500-year flood level. Multiple roads and bridges around Traverse City and elsewhere within the county were periodically closed, either due to failures/sinkholes or to reassess roadway conditions following heavy rains. Evacuations occurred throughout the county, including the Kingsley and Mayfield areas, and 8 people were rescued by boat near Mayfield, with several floating propane tanks also secured for safety purposes. Damage estimates in Grand Traverse county alone exceeded $15 million, after only 20 percent of road and infrastructure assessments completed by mid-May. No known injuries or fatalities due to flooding were reported as of mid-May.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding impacts began around the 12th, with road closures due to shoulder failures and complete culvert and roadway failures beginning around the 14th along the Manistee River, including North Highbridge Rd near the Manistee River. Flooding impacted the Northern Michigan Dragway in Kaleva, delaying its season opener from April 18 to the 25th due to flooding of the track. The Tippy Dam near Wellston on the Manistee River saw high flows; the cooperative observing site at this location recorded a total of 15.68 inches of liquid precipitation for the month of April, with almost half of this falling between the 12th and 15th. This was nearly 3 times the previous highest rainfall for the month of April at this location -- 6.60in in 1929, and the highest monthly total out of all months on record for this location. Consistent records began in 1927.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant flooding impacts were noted in the Cadillac, MI area, where 10-15 inches of rainfall countywide through the first half of the month resulted in lake levels on Lakes Cadillac and Mitchell rising 2 ft during the month, peaking on the 19th; the previous lake level record, set in 2008, was broken by 6 inches on the 13th and an additional 5-6in rise was noted the following day. This resulted in damage to even first floors of homes, property, and roadways, with standing water still present in some areas well into June. The wastewater treatment facilities for the city of Cadillac were also impacted by the flooding, with high water levels diminishing effectiveness of sewer lift pumps:  the sanitary sewage depth levels at the lift station at Division and Leeson St. were 20-25ft deep, compared to a normal 4-5ft depth. A state of emergency was declared for the city of Cadillac on the 15th. Some city parks began to open by the 22nd, though high water levels remained. Elsewhere in the county, the Hodenpyl Dam near Mesick on the Manistee River also required some preventative reinforcement on the 16th; the river was up to the base of the M-37 bridge deck over the Manistee River near Sherman, and there was concern about closing multiple Manistee River crossing sites, which would have severely impacted north-south travel across the county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant flooding impacts across Presque Isle county in northeast Lower Michigan, including the eastern section of Black Lake that is within Presque Isle county, resulting in a state of emergency declaration. Several main roads took severe washout damage, including M-68 near Ocqueoc Falls, where a temporary repair was completed by early summer to limp the area through until a full repair could be done in October, causing significant issues for Presque Isle road commission project logistics and planning. Heythaler Highway near Rogers City also suffered severe roadway failure. As of mid June, the Michigan DOT estimate for repairs for the northern Michigan region was at least $6.6 million. The Rogers City wastewater treatment plant, designed to handle 1 million gallons of wastewater per day, was overrun with over twice that on average during the mid-month heavy rains, placing the plant in jeopardy of failure, and residents of the city were asked to reduce water use for this reason.

Traverse City, Houghton Lake, and Gaylord all recorded their wettest Aprils on record. Coupled with thawing ground and saturated soils, this resulted in widespread historic flooding across all of the northern Lower Peninsula. 20 USGS river gauges in the region set new all-time records, most of which broke the previous records by 1-2 feet. This, too, resulted in enhanced concern for multiple high-impact dams to be overtopped, including the Cheboygan Dam in the town of Cheboygan, which reached a height of just under 6 inches from the top at its peak, and the Bellaire Dam in northwest Lower Michigan. Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.

Water rescues had to be performed near Stoney Creek on the southeast side of Danville as the creek overflowed its banks and flooded a few homes.

Many inland lake levels further upstream in the Cheboygan River basin were also well above normal, resulting in damage from flooding and ice shoves as winds pushed chunks of floating ice into homes along the shores; the high groundwater content and high water levels also caused widespread impacts to public and private water supplies and wastewater treatment facilities. Multiple portions of multiple roads also failed during this period, including M-119, the Tunnel of Trees, a famous tourist route along the Lake Michigan coastline between Harbor Springs and Cross Village, and the heavily-trafficked Beitner Rd Bridge south of Traverse City on the Boardman River; the river gauge at this latter location was also swept away when the culverts and roadway failed. Portions of roads that received damage are likely to remain closed for months. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, was closed from April 11 until May 5th due to significant flooding over the runways; the airport did not return to full operations for both runways until June 1. By April 15th, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer had declared a state of emergency for 21 counties in northern Michigan within the WFO Gaylord, MI forecast area; President Donald Trump issued a Major Disaster Declaration for these same counties on June 30th. Total flood damage estimates as of July 2026 exceeded $800 million.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to 1.5 inches of warm rain fell on remaining snowpack across the Central Brooks range resulting in a rapid rise of the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River between Coldfoot and Wiseman. Late evening on Monday the 15th, the public reported that water was moving over the road to Wiseman. A social media comment on the NWS Warning post came in just after midnight on the 16th stating that the water was high enough that it would be very difficult if not impossible to get in or out of Wiseman by road. In addition the NWS received reports from the general public stating that the water came up very fast, but did begin to slowly subside through the day on the 16th as the rain tapered off and came to an end.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Middle June saw a disturbance track over the Central Brooks Range resulting in anywhere from 1 to 1.5 inches of rain in about a 24 hour period. While most rivers were ice free, plenty of snowpack remained across the higher slopes. With high temperatures generally in the 60's and overnight lows remaining above freezing, excessive snowmelt combined with heavy rainfall lead to rapid rises along area streams and rivers, including the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River. As a result, flooding was reported from Coldfoot to Wiseman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front stationed across northern Pennsylvania began to slowly sag southward during the daytime hours on July 10, 2026. This, coupled with sufficient instability and moisture over central Pennsylvania allowed for scattered instances of showers and thunderstorm to form across portions of central Pennsylvania. Storm motion parallel to the front allowed for training of thunderstorms, which allowed for isolated instances of flash flooding during the afternoon and evening hours in Centre, Cambria, and Blair Counties where soil was already saturated from recent heavy rainfall. Given the lack of bulk shear, thunderstorms largely stayed sub-severe outside of a thunderstorm in northern Northumberland County that became marginally severe with numerous reports of tree damage in and around Turbotsville.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours of June 5, 2026, thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across southern Richardson County. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 1.50 to 3.00 inches per hour, driving estimated total rainfall to between 4.00 and 6.00 inches. As a result, the Big Nemaha River gauge at Falls City (FLLN1) rose above flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge crested at 31.09 ft, consistent with moderate flooding, at 11:28 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge fell below flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 6th.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough descended into the northeast quadrant of the United States while a surface low ambled east across Ontario and Quebec. Severe thunderstorms produced two main swaths of damage across the area. The first swath of damage encompassed areas along and north of a line from Wood County east to Randolph County, while the second was primarily concentrated along and near the I-64 corridor. In addition to numerous reports of downed trees and power outages, some notable areas of damage were determined to be the result of tornadoes. One EF-0, two EF-1, and three EF-2 tornadoes were confirmed by post-event damage surveys. ||Three of the six confirmed tornadoes     the EF-0 in Barbour, EF-1 in Randolph, and EF-2 in southern Ritchie     were short-lived with tracks under two miles long. The other three tornadoes originated in Washington County Ohio and then progressed across the Ohio River into West Virginia. Two of these three were EF-2s, with tracks around 12 miles long, that ended in Pleasants County. The third, an EF-1, traveled through parts of Pleasants, Tyler, and Ritchie, before concluding its 24 mile journey in Doddridge County.||Heavy downpours produced a stripe of two to three inches of rain across Lincoln, Boone, Kanawha, and Fayette Counties, which prompted some flash flooding. Meanwhile, rainfall amounts exceeding two inches led to additional flooding across the north-central parts of the state. Four to nearly eight inches of rain produced catastrophic flash flooding across portions of Lewis, Upshur, and Randolph Counties. Numerous reports detailed impassable or washed out roads, water rescues, and homes and businesses being inundated by flood waters. Even a portion of I-79 was shut down due to flooding. In Upshur County, two individuals perished when their vehicle was swept off the road and submerged in flood waters. Extensive damage was caused by this thousand year flood event, with clean up and restoration efforts continuing well into the summer of 2026.||Flash flooding eventually gave way to river flooding as excessive runoff made its way into local rivers, creeks, and streams. Gauges recorded flooding on the West Fork River, Buckhannon River, Sand Run, Tygart Valley River, South Fork Hughes River, and Middle Island Creek. The gauges at Buckhannon and Sand Run both recorded major flooding, while the Audra, Clarksburg,  Ellamore, Little, and Philippi gauges each peaked in moderate flood stage. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Big Sioux River near Castlewood went into flood on the afternoon of July 9th as a result of multiple rounds of thunderstorms that delivered heavy rainfall across the southern Sisseton hills region on the evening of July 7th into the morning hours July 8th. The river crested at 9.26 feet, or 0.26 feet above flood stage during the early morning hours of July 10th and fell below flood later that morning. This level resulted in water over the culvert on 184th Street and the flooding of agricultural lands north of the town of Castlewood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high-water rescue occurred at the Black Bear Creek crossing amidst a period of prolonged flooding. The event time is estimated based on information from first responders.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Batesville area was impacted by flooding along the Leona River triggered by heavy rain concentrated in Uvalde County north of Batesville. Initial rises on the Leona River on July 16 flooded portions of US57 near Batesville. A much more significant rise occurred in the early morning of July 17, when floodwaters along the Leona River reached the community between 0000 and 0200CST, causing widespread flooding.||Inundation spread across much of the eastern half of Batesville and extended to FM117, impacting many residences east and some west of the highway. The greatest inundation extent was observed in southeastern portions of Batesville, where floodwaters reached a    mile away from the Leona River. Flooding was observed along Main Street, Old Loma Vista Road, and adjacent roads. Around 70 families reported flood damage to their homes and belongings, with water levels reaching as high as 3ft inside. Approximately 120 people relocated to shelters. While floodwaters reached Batesville School, the campus sustained minimal damage. Batesville was isolated due to the flooding and subsequent closures of US57, FM117, and other surrounding roads.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A major flood wave on the Nueces River triggered by torrential rain primarily over Uvalde County moved into Dimmit County on July 17 and caused extensive inundation of the floodplain in Dimmit County. Satellite imagery indicated the width of inundation spanned up to 2 miles in width over the lower Nueces River and along Soldier Slough. The Nueces River at Asherton remained at Major flood stage between July 17 and July 24, recording a crest of 31.56ft on July 18.||Damage to public infrastructure in Dimmit County amounted to around $1.4 million with damage primarily wrought to roadway infrastructure, water control facilities, and other utilities. Twenty-eight homes in the county were damaged or destroyed. The greatest amount of inundation in residential areas occurred in the Espantosa Subdivision and areas around Midway Park, where mandatory evacuations were ordered. Several roads in Dimmit County were closed due to flooding including FM65, FM189, FM1019, FM1433, and Highway 85. Flood damage to water wells resulted in a water shortage in Carrizo Springs with water service disruptions continuing into mid-August.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low amplitude trough was swinging through the Midwest with an associated surface boundary draped across southern Iowa. A pool of 3000+ J/kg MLCAPE developed along and south of the boundary with mid-level lapse rates of 7+ C/km while effective shear was around 30 kts. As the low-level jet increased through the evening, convergence along the boundary resulted in storm development across southern Iowa. Severe wind gusts and large hail of up to two inches in diameter were reported with the storms. These storms trained along the boundary and resulted in heavy rain amounts of two to five inches, causing flash flooding in Marion County. Rural portions of southern Marion County experienced prolonged flooding that lasted through the morning of June 8th. Roads were closed in and around Cedar and English creeks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second round of severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of July 7 across northern and northeast South Dakota. Peak wind gusts included 72 mph in Akaska (Walworth County), 71 mph at the South Dakota State University mesonet station 10 miles west-southwest of Aberdeen, 70 mph at the South Dakota State University mesonet station seven miles south of Claremont, and 68 mph at the Aberdeen Regional Airport Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) all in Brown County. Hail to the size of quarters was observed 5 miles west of the town of Webster (Day County) and in the town of Selby (Walworth County). ||Heavy rainfall was observed across northeast South Dakota, which resulted in flash flooding and river flooding. 5.18 inches was recorded by the CoCoRaHS observer in Claremont, the COOP observer in Webster observed 4.72 inches, and the automated COOP station at Sand Lake logged 4.39 inches. Many of the COOP and CoCoRaHS observers from in and around Aberdeen and points east in Day, Marshall and Grant counties recorded around 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rainfall. Around 2 inches of rain was recorded by the COOP and CoCoRaHS observers in and around the Watertown area as well. ||Flash flooding struck Aberdeen, stranding multiple vehicles in water near 24th Avenue Northwest (Fairgrounds Road). Streets underwater by as much as 1 foot were reported  primarily on the north side of town and eroding storm sewer infrastructure created a sinkhole at 1st Avenue Northeast and North Pennsylvania Avenue. The Marshall county Emergency Manager relayed that flooding around Newport Colony had resulted in roads under water and washouts. Runoff triggered river flooding along Moccasin Creek, Mud Creek, Willow Creek, the South Branch Tributary of Mud Creek, and the Big Sioux River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.  Two brief tornadoes also occurred, one in Rawlins County the other near Menlo.  No damage was reported with these tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough moved across the Central Plains and into the Midwest early on the morning of June 10th, while a strong low-level jet helped trigger convection across Nebraska. As the storms tracked into central Iowa, a weaker cap allowed for strengthening and a bowing segment resulted in gusts of 60-70 mph. A midday lull followed, allowing skies to clear and instability to build, with a plume of 4000 J/kg MLCAPE. Effective bulk shear of 45-50 knots helped organize updrafts, initially favoring a supercellular storm mode as storm redeveloped in the late afternoon. By evening, the storms grew upscale into multicell cluster. Storms produced damaging wind gusts and hail up to two inches in diameter. A tornado touched down in southern Davis County, causing tree damage. Additionally, torrential rainfall led to road closures across Marion, Monroe, Appanoose, and Davis counties.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Little Minnesota River near Peever went into flood during the morning hours of July 31st, but only stayed in flood for an hour and a half, cresting at 17.06 or 0.06 feet above flood stage.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms produced heavy rainfall on July 30th into the early morning of July 31st, with a number of reports of rainfall at or in excess of 5 inches centered across Day and Roberts counties. Heavy rainfall resulted in flooding and stalled cars in the city of Aberdeen with the Official National Weather Service observation of 2.55 inches. Flooding also impacted the cities of Pierre and Fort Pierre including portions of US Highway 14. Multiple roads and county/state highways were closed north of US Highway 12 in Day county due to water over the road, including Highway 33 near Roslyn and Highway 27 near Pierpont. The highest reported measured total was 6.90 inches by the CoCoRaHS observer 6.6 miles east northeast of Grenville (Day County).||There was also a brief period of minor flooding along the Little Minnesota River near Peever, after 5.8 inches was recorded by the COOP observer in Sisseton, and 6.34 was measured by the CoCoRaHS observer 10 miles east northeast of Sisseton.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain in the morning renewed flooding across portions of Appanoose, Monroe, Lucas, and Wayne counties with stream continuing to rise due to the combination of new rain and run off from earlier rain. Impacts were worst in the southwest half of Monroe county with numerous road closures across the area.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed early on the morning of June 11th as a shortwave lifted out of Kansas into Iowa, fueled by a low-level jet and racing across southern Iowa along a remnant outflow boundary from the previous evening's convection. The storms quickly grew upscale into a robust mesoscale convective system (MCS), producing widespread damaging winds and hail up to two inches in diameter across the southern half of the state. Intense straight-line winds of 80 to 100 mph associated with bowing segments within the squall line caused severe tree, structural, and crop damage. Some of the hardest-hit areas included western Adams County, central Dallas County, and a corridor spanning southern Union, northern Ringgold, southern Clarke, and northern Decatur counties   where intense straight-line winds combined with wind-driven hail. Tragically, a man in Des Moines was killed when a tree fell on him during the storm. One tornado also touched down in Adams County, causing substantial damage to a home and power poles along its path. Additionally, torrential rain fell over areas that had already received heavy precipitation the previous day. This led to renewed flooding, particularly along English Creek and Cedar Creek in Marion County, where floodwaters took several days to recede.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The bridge on CR30E between 130S and 140S had enough flood water over it that the bridge was blocked by debris and not passable.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.  Two brief tornadoes also occurred, one in Rawlins County the other near Menlo.  No damage was reported with these tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unprecedented heavy rain event/rain storm impacted eastern NY on July 28-30, 2026. Scattered to numerous instances of flash flooding occurred with the Greater Capital Region, eastern Catskills and northern portions of the mid-Hudson Valley being the hardest hit. ||A closed/cutoff low was positioned over the region. The mid and upper low captured a double-barrel low pressure system with one low centered over eastern/southern NY and a secondary coastal low southeast of Long Island. Meso-vortices migrated around the mid and upper level low over the region. A tremendous fetch of deep moisture occurred from the Atlantic and Gulf. Precipitable water anomalies were 2-3 standard deviations above normal in the 1.40-1.80 inch range. Freezing levels were high in the 11-13 kft above ground level range. Very efficient rainfall processes occurred with more of a cool season style synoptic system with an impressive stratiform rainband with initially embedded convection in the low/mid level deformation zone of the system. Intense rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour and thunderstorms/heavy showers repeatedly moved over the same areas, mainly during the early morning hours on July 29. The Greater Capital Region, northern reaches of the mid-Hudson Valley and eastern Catskills received the most rainfall with widespread amounts of 6 to 12 inches.||Impressive, record-breaking rainfall amounts occurred in a 2-day stretch, though most of the rainfall occurred in a 24-30 hour period. 5.45 inches of rain occurred on July 29th at Albany, shattering the old record of 1.90 inches set in 1974. This was also the wettest July day on record for Albany. This calendar day total is the 2nd wettest day on record overall, only behind the 5.60 inches that occurred on Sept 16, 1999 with TS Floyd moisture. The 2-day total at Albany was 7.00 inches.||The NYS Mesonet network recorded 11.79 inches of rainfall at Schodack and 11.47 inches at Kinderhook.  This was a 1 in a 1000 year precipitation/heavy rain event for those areas. Poughkeepsie also had 2.68 of rainfall on July 29th which broke the old record of 1.86 in 1971.||As a result, 9 States of Emergency orders were issued at the town/municipality level (Schodack, Coxsackie, Hunter, Windham, Greenville, Shandanken, Stuyvesant, Chatham, and Germantown); 3 States of Emergency orders were issued at the county level (Rensselaer, Greene, and Columbia); and 3 counties had evacuation shelters opened by the American Red Cross (Albany, Columbia, and Greene). Additionally, Saratoga County reported 50 homes that had basement flooding and had to be pumped out. ||Despite this much rainfall, abnormally dry conditions ahead of this event limited impacts from river flooding. Only five river points reached flood stage (4 Minor and one Moderate) during this event with one river falling just short of minor flood stage (Mt Marion on the Esopus).||Preceding this heavy rainfall event were a few localized severe thunderstorms which downed some trees and wires during the afternoon hours on July 28.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms stationed across central Pennsylvania and southern New York during the late evening hours of July 27, 2026 continued to exhibit signs of strengthening as they continued into July 28th. This trend was due to there being sufficient instability for storms to continue to sustain themselves as they continued overnight into the 28th. A severe thunderstorm north of the Pennsylvania-New York border moved south of the border during the late evening hours and produced a severe wind gust at Bradford Regional Airport; however, no damage was observed with this storm. Similarly, a severe thunderstorm stationed across central Pennsylvania moves southward into Adams County, where tree damage was observed during the early morning hours of July 28th. Winds parallel to storm motion allowed for multiple rounds of heavy rainfall for locations, with considerable flash flooding beginning during the morning hours of July 28th in McKean County. The communities of Eldred and Lewis Run were hit especially hard with flooding with multiple businesses and multiple roadways taking on over one foot of water. As these storms shifted southward, similarly flooding was observed in the town of Coalport, where multiple streets were under one foot of water and there were reported water rescues in the town due to stranded cars during the early afternoon hours. Breaks in the cloud deck occurred further southeast during the morning and early afternoon hours, allowing for thunderstorms to become strong-to-severe quickly across the southern tier of Pennsylvania, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Cumberland, Dauphin, York, Adams, and Franklin Counties. Due to saturated soils, isolated instances of flash flooding was observed in Lebanon County along with more widespread flooding in the town of Waynesboro in Franklin County where multiple roadways were closed due to rising water.
