EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.

Scattered to numerous instances of flash flooding occurred with the Greater Capital Region, eastern Catskills and northern portions of the mid-Hudson Valley being the hardest hit. ||A closed/cutoff low was positioned over the region. The mid and upper low captured a double-barrel low pressure system with one low centered over eastern/southern NY and a secondary coastal low southeast of Long Island. Meso-vortices migrated around the mid and upper level low over the region. A tremendous fetch of deep moisture occurred from the Atlantic and Gulf. Precipitable water anomalies were 2-3 standard deviations above normal in the 1.40-1.80 inch range. Freezing levels were high in the 11-13 kft above ground level range. Very efficient rainfall processes occurred with more of a cool season style synoptic system with an impressive stratiform rainband with initially embedded convection in the low/mid level deformation zone of the system. Intense rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour and thunderstorms/heavy showers repeatedly moved over the same areas, mainly during the early morning hours on July 29. The Greater Capital Region, northern reaches of the mid-Hudson Valley and eastern Catskills received the most rainfall with widespread amounts of 6 to 12 inches.||Impressive, record-breaking rainfall amounts occurred in a 2-day stretch, though most of the rainfall occurred in a 24-30 hour period. 5.45 inches of rain occurred on July 29th at Albany, shattering the old record of 1.90 inches set in 1974. This was also the wettest July day on record for Albany. This calendar day total is the 2nd wettest day on record overall, only behind the 5.60 inches that occurred on Sept 16, 1999 with TS Floyd moisture. The 2-day total at Albany was 7.00 inches.||The NYS Mesonet network recorded 11.79 inches of rainfall at Schodack and 11.47 inches at Kinderhook.  This was a 1 in a 1000 year precipitation/heavy rain event for those areas. Poughkeepsie also had 2.68 of rainfall on July 29th which broke the old record of 1.86 in 1971.||As a result, 9 States of Emergency orders were issued at the town/municipality level (Schodack, Coxsackie, Hunter, Windham, Greenville, Shandanken, Stuyvesant, Chatham, and Germantown); 3 States of Emergency orders were issued at the county level (Rensselaer, Greene, and Columbia); and 3 counties had evacuation shelters opened by the American Red Cross (Albany, Columbia, and Greene). Additionally, Saratoga County reported 50 homes that had basement flooding and had to be pumped out. ||Despite this much rainfall, abnormally dry conditions ahead of this event limited impacts from river flooding. Only five river points reached flood stage (4 Minor and one Moderate) during this event with one river falling just short of minor flood stage (Mt Marion on the Esopus).||Preceding this heavy rainfall event were a few localized severe thunderstorms which downed some trees and wires during the afternoon hours on July 28.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Shortwave energy rotating around an upper-level trough over the Northeast interacted with an unseasonably humid (dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s   F). Afternoon heating yielded moderate Surface-Based CAPE (SBCAPE) across southern and central New Hampshire.  Abundant precipitable water (PWAT) combined with relatively weak mid-level steering flow created an environment optimized for slow-moving, high-efficiency rainfall cores and localized wet microbursts.  Localized wet microbursts led to some tree damage along with some urban flood issues.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of heavy rain resulted in moderate flooding and severe, accelerated riverbank erosion in Talkeetna, prompting a preemptive local emergency disaster declaration by the Mat-Su Borough Assembly. Rapid bank erosion threatened approximately eight riverfront structures, including four primary residences and two businesses, leaving one residence in imminent danger of collapsing into the river. An outbuilding was lost, and approximately 30 feet of bank washed away near Susitna River Lodging within a 48-hour period. Significant erosion also destroyed approximately 40 feet of the BLM runway, while floodwaters inundated areas near Main Street and forced the borough to close the Talkeetna River campground. Further damage included road washouts along Cummings and Beaver Roads, and a landslide that halted Alaska Railroad service north of the town. The flooding was driven by 4 to 6 inches of rainfall concentrated over the Talkeetna Mountains between July 19 and July 23. This produced a crest of 13.07 feet on the upstream Talkeetna River gage (TRTA2), 14.25 feet at the Talkeetna River railroad bridge gage (TKTA2), and 24.20 feet on the Susitna River (SUNA2).
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low-pressure system originating in the Bering Sea moved across mainland Alaska in mid-to-late July 2026, bringing multiple rounds of anomalous, heavy rainfall to Southcentral Alaska that approached record levels for the month. Between July 13 and July 23, persistent wet conditions saturated the region, with the heaviest precipitation focused over the Talkeetna Mountains and the Susitna Valley. The Talkeetna River Basin received 4 to 6 inches of rain, or a 5- to 10-year average recurrence interval. Meanwhile the Yentna Basin saw 10-day totals of 6 to 8 inches. This excessive runoff caused fast-responding rivers and streams to swell, leading to moderate flooding, severe riverbank erosion, road washouts, and a local emergency disaster declaration by the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused Moose Creek to rise rapidly, surpassing the minor flood stage of 16.5 feet on the Moose Creek at Oilwell Road stream gage. By the morning of July 23, the river stage reached 16.55 feet, and an estimated 1.5 feet of water was flowing over Oilwell Road due to a culvert issue, rendering the road impassable for cars and blocking access to the stream gage. Water levels on Moose Creek were the highest recorded since 2006. By 11:00 AM on July 24, water levels had receded enough for vehicles to travel the road again, though an observer reported that approximately 60 feet of the road surface on the southwest approach to the bridge remained flooded into the late afternoon.   The flooding was driven by localized heavy rainfall, with three-day totals varying between 2.90 inches at the Tokositna Snotel site and 3.59 inches at Talkeetna.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three rounds of heavy rainfall over a 10-day period resulted in moderate flooding on the Yentna River at Lake Creek. During this event, moderate flooding impacted numerous lodges and properties in the Lake Creek area, with reports of up to 1 foot of water inside structures. High-water marks at McDougal Lodge were estimated to be nearly 3 feet lower than the record flood of August 2025, resulting in substantially less severe structural impacts than the previous year.   Between July 13 and July 23, the Yentna Basin received 6 to 8 inches of rainfall, representing a 10- to 25-year return interval for 10-day precipitation totals. This series of storms caused three distinct river crests: the first storm produced 2 to 3 inches of rain and a crest of 21.17 feet on July 15; a second storm brought an additional 2 to 4 inches of rain, cresting at 21.89 feet on July 21; and a final storm dropped around 2 inches of rain, pushing the river to a moderate flood crest of 21.95 feet on July 23.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous impacts were observed in the Albany, Guilderland, Colonie, and Rensselaer areas as a result of prolonged, heavy rainfall. Swiftwater rescue crews evacuated one adult and two children from flood waters affecting homes in Guilderland. The American Red Cross opened a shelter in Albany County where severe flooding affected at least twenty families. Evacuations were also conducted in Colonie, though the exact number is unknown. Finally, the Department of Environmental Conservation dam safety staff at Rensselaer Lake Dam activated the emergency action plan in the non-failure condition due to water elevation that was 2 feet from the crest of the dam. The low-level outlet was therefore opened to prevent water levels from continuing to rise at the structure.
